Neurology · published research

ADHD

A published sham-controlled study reported improved impulse-control and 2-back task performance and higher acute prefrontal oxygenation after tPBM. A small unreviewed sham-controlled crossover preprint also reported better working-memory task scores. A separate seven-day, single-arm study found task-score gains, but no study has shown a change in ADHD symptoms or everyday functioning.

Publications and records

3unique peer-reviewed publications

Publication and study types

Human randomized sham-controlled study: 1 (two-stage)

Human single-arm study: 1 (n=48)

Rat experiment: 1

Additional preprint, not peer reviewed and excluded from total: 1 human sham-controlled crossover (n=28 with ADHD; 29 healthy controls)

No systematic reviews or meta-analyses identified

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study identified

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Acute impulse-control task (Salehpour et al., 2026): 51% more Conners CPT correct rejections versus sham in the ADHD subgroup (p=0.017; Cohen's d=0.93). In the second stage (n=52), 2-back correct rejections improved (p=0.040); fNIRS oxyhemoglobin and total hemoglobin increased (p=0.011 and p=0.038, respectively). No standardized effect sizes were reported for those outcomes.

Working-memory task (Yuan et al., 2026 preprint): K-score increase after active versus sham tPBM (n=28; within-group Cohen's d=0.479; FDR p=0.026). Not peer reviewed.

Uncontrolled seven-day study (Lai et al., 2025): working-memory and attention task gains, with peak within-group Cohen's d=0.84–1.26 at two to three weeks. Without a comparator, these estimates do not isolate a PBM effect.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term impulse-control task performance and acute prefrontal oxygenation

Low for short-term working-memory task performance

Low for sustained attention, core ADHD symptoms, and everyday function

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A published sham-controlled study reported improved impulse-control and 2-back task performance and higher acute prefrontal oxygenation after tPBM. A small unreviewed sham-controlled crossover preprint also reported better working-memory task scores. A separate seven-day, single-arm study found task-score gains, but no study has shown a change in ADHD symptoms or everyday functioning.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact ADHD category contains three unique peer-reviewed publications: one two-stage randomized sham-controlled human study, one human single-arm study, and one rat experiment. A recent September 2026 human preprint is noted separately and is not included in the database count. Human outcomes are cognitive-task performance and physiological measurements, not long-term symptoms or daily function.

Human and clinical evidence

The published 2026 randomized, sham-controlled study enrolled 223 adults with and without a reported ADHD history in its first stage. Within the ADHD group, active tPBM led to a 51% increase in Conners Continuous Performance Test (CPT) correct rejections versus sham (p=0.017; Cohen's d=0.93). In its second stage, 52 adults with ADHD were randomized to active or sham. After one eight-minute 1064-nm treatment, active tPBM improved 2-back correct rejections (p=0.040) and increased prefrontal oxyhemoglobin (p=0.011) and total hemoglobin (p=0.038). These are acute task and fNIRS outcomes, not evidence of symptom control. ADHD status relied on a self-reported prior diagnosis and a screening scale rather than a structured diagnostic interview (Salehpour et al., 2026).

A separate single-arm study treated 48 adults for 12 minutes daily over seven days. N-back working-memory and Continuous Performance Test-Identical Pairs (CPT-IP) scores improved, with within-group peak effect sizes of d=0.84–1.26 at two to three weeks after treatment. With no sham or untreated group, practice, expectation, and time effects cannot be excluded (Lai et al., 2025).

A medRxiv preprint posted in September 2026 studied 28 young adults with ADHD in a double-blind sham-controlled crossover, with 29 healthy controls as a reference group. Each participant received one 16-minute active 1064-nm session and one sham session over the right prefrontal cortex, separated by at least a week. Working-memory K scores increased after active stimulation (within-group Cohen's d=0.479; FDR-corrected p=0.026). The preprint has not been peer reviewed, so this finding needs independent confirmation (Yuan et al., 2026, preprint).

Animal evidence

In spontaneously hypertensive rats, daily 808-nm PBM for 21 days reduced open-field distance and movement speed compared with sham, while prefrontal fractional anisotropy increased and Iba-1-positive microglia decreased. The study also reported preservation of myelin in ADHD-related regions. These behavioral and tissue findings come from one rat model and do not establish a human dose or effect (Huang et al., 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell or ex-vivo study is classified in the ADHD category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The published and preprint human studies used 1064-nm near-infrared laser light over the right prefrontal cortex. The 2026 published study used a continuous-wave HD Laser (Cell Gen Therapeutics LLC) at 3.4 W and 250 mW/cm² for eight minutes total, alternating between two right-forehead sites. This delivered 60 J/cm² at each site during its four-minute exposure. The 48-person uncontrolled study used seven daily 12-minute sessions; its report does not name the device model. The 2026 preprint used 150 mW/cm² for 16 minutes in one active session, with a Jieliang handheld laser; its model is not stated. The rat experiment used 808-nm near-infrared light for 25 seconds daily. These protocols do not establish an optimal schedule or durable clinical benefit.

Interpretation

The published sham-controlled comparison found acute improvements on an impulse-control task, a 2-back task, and prefrontal oxygenation. A small unreviewed crossover preprint reported a working-memory task gain, while one uncontrolled study reported later cognitive-test gains and one rat experiment found behavioral and tissue changes. No study has established improvement in core ADHD symptoms or day-to-day functioning.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

A published sham-controlled study found better correct-rejection performance after one session, with a large effect in adults reporting ADHD. Its second 52-person stage also found a 2-back task signal and higher prefrontal hemoglobin. A separate 28-person sham-controlled crossover preprint reported a modest working-memory K-score gain, but it has not been peer reviewed. Repeated-session findings come from an uncontrolled 48-person study. No study establishes improvement in core symptoms or daily function; independent controlled replication is needed.
